title_prefix: RBF descendant expansion runs before the
mechanism: CHECK-RBF-RULES binds (replaced (%rbf-replaced-set mempool direct-conflicts)) in its opening LET (src/mempool/mempool.lisp:1282-1283) and only then, in the body, consults %rbf-cluster-caps (:1285-1287). %rbf-replaced-set (:1217-1225) walks mempool-descendants for EVERY direct conflict, so the full eviction set is materialised before rule 5 has had a chance to reject the replacement. Core's GetEntriesForConflicts (refs/bitcoin/src/policy/rbf.cpp:58-82 at d3056bc) does the opposite and says why: GetUniqueClusterCount is tested against MAX_REPLACEMENT_CANDIDATES and returns the error string first, and only after that does the CalculateDescendants loop run, under the comment 'The cluster count limit ensures that we won't do too much work on a single invocation of this function.' The same inversion is in CHECK-PACKAGE-RBF-RULES (:1336-1344), whose LET also expands descendants before the aggregate rule-5 check. The RBF staging rewrite now on main did NOT change this: it replaced the diagram staging (txgraph-rbf-diagrams, copying the affected clusters), which runs later in the body at :1307-1314, and left the LET/cap order untouched.
consequence: Wasted work on a replacement rule 5 is about to reject, and the work is attacker-chosen: the number of direct conflicts is bounded only by the candidate's input count (find-rbf-conflicts, src/mempool/mempool.lisp:1190-1202, walks every input and has no cap of its own, matching Core), and each conflict drags in up to its whole 64-transaction cluster. Measured 0.012 s of descendant expansion for 200 conflicts spanning 12800 mempool transactions before the cap returned :too-many-clusters; the cap check itself was below timer resolution. A maximum-standard-weight transaction can carry roughly 1400-2400 inputs, so against fully populated clusters the wasted expansion extrapolates to order 0.1 s per rejected message, held under the node lock (validate-transaction-for-mempool reaches check-rbf-rules at src/validation/transaction.lisp:1218-1221). That ceiling is low enough that this is hygiene rather than a denial of service on its own, so S3 -- but it removes exactly the guarantee Core's ordering was written to provide, and the cost scales with mempool population, which an attacker also influences.
evidence: Container /Users/sen/common-lisp/bl-ga11v-misc-s3a, warm image, against src/mempool/mempool.lisp as it stands after the RBF staging rewrite. Probe build/ga11probe/p-rbf-order.lisp builds 200 independent chains of 64 transactions (12800 entries) with bitcoin-lisp.mempool:*txgraph-shadow-checks* bound to NIL, then times the two helpers separately over the 200 chain roots: (:mempool-txs 12800 :direct-conflicts 200 :replaced-set-size 12800 :descendant-expansion-secs 0.012 :cluster-cap-secs 0.0 :cap-verdict :too-many-clusters). Probe build/ga11probe/p-rbf-trace.lisp then proves the ORDER at the real entry point rather than by reading source: with %rbf-replaced-set and %rbf-cluster-caps traced, check-rbf-rules on the same pool returns (NIL :too-many-clusters NIL) and the trace stream carries %RBF-REPLACED-SET entry at offset 28 and exit at 28296, both before %RBF-CLUSTER-CAPS entry at 28411 and exit at 56679 -- the expansion completes before the cap is consulted, and the cap then rejects. Core side read at d3056bc: rbf.cpp:58-82, including the ordering comment at :77-79.
fix_shape: Reorder so rule 5 gates the expansion, which is the whole point of Core's arrangement. In CHECK-RBF-RULES drop REPLACED out of the opening LET, run the %rbf-cluster-caps test first and return :too-many-clusters there, then bind REPLACED with LET* (or an inner LET) before the spends-conflicting-tx scan that is its first consumer; do the same in CHECK-PACKAGE-RBF-RULES at src/mempool/mempool.lisp:1336-1344. Nothing else moves: rules 3 and 4, the disjointness check and the diagram staging all keep their current positions and their inputs. Note that %rbf-cluster-caps already takes DIRECT-CONFLICTS, not the expanded set, so it needs no change at all -- the fix is purely the binding position. Beware the trap this shape encodes: a LET binding is not a statement that runs where the guard reads, and a green suite cannot see the difference because the verdict is identical either way. The regression test therefore has to observe the ORDER, not the result -- trace or instrument the two helpers and assert the cap is consulted first, or assert that a rejected-by-rule-5 candidate leaves the descendant walk uncalled, with a passing candidate as the positive control so the assertion cannot hold vacuously.
